1:1.headline: Same word twice: full of people, then great among nations
1:1.body: רבתי appears twice in the verse. Rashi says the first means 'full of people'. Ibn Ezra says the second is different: it means 'great', a noble among the nations, as in 'the king's nobles'.

sources.quote: רַבָּתִי עָם. יוּ"ד יְתֵרָה, כְּמוֹ "רַבַּת עָם", שֶׁהָיְתָה עַמָּהּ רַב
sources.says: Rashi says the י is extra and the first רבתי means her people were many.

sources.quote: רבתי בגוים – איננה כראשונה, רק בלשון גדולה, כמו: "ורבי המלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the second רבתי is not like the first; it means greatness, as in 'the king's nobles'.

1:1.headline: 'Like a widow', but her husband is coming back
1:1.body: Rashi stops on the word 'like'. Jerusalem is not truly a widow. She is like a wife whose husband went overseas and means to return to her.

sources.quote: וְלֹא אַלְמָנָה מַמָּשׁ, אֶלָּא כְאִשָּׁה שֶׁהָלַךְ בַּעְלָהּ לִמְדִינַת הַיָּם וְדַעְתּוֹ לַחֲזוֹר אֶצְלָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says she is not really a widow, but like a woman whose husband went overseas intending to come back to her.

1:2.headline: 'Weeping, she weeps': one cry for each Temple
1:2.body: The verb is doubled: 'weeping, she weeps'. Rashi says there are two weepings, for the two destructions of the Temple.

sources.quote: בָּכוֹ תִבְכֶּה. שְׁתֵּי בְכִיּוֹת עַל שְׁתֵּי חֻרְבָּנִין
sources.says: Rashi says the doubled verb means two weepings for two destructions.

1:2.headline: Why 'at night'? Rashi gives three reasons
1:2.body: Rashi says the Temple burned at night. Or: the night Israel wept over the spies' report, on the ninth of Av, brought this on. Or: when someone cries at night, whoever hears cries too.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַמִּקְדָּשׁ נִשְׂרַף בַּלַּיְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says the Temple was burned at night.

sources.quote: לַיְלָה שֶׁל בְּכִיַּת מְרַגְּלִים בְּתִשְׁעָה בְאָב גָּרְמָה לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the night of weeping over the spies, on the ninth of Av, caused it.

sources.quote: שֶׁכָּל הַבּוֹכֶה בַלַּיְלָה, הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ קוֹלוֹ בּוֹכֶה עִמּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says whoever cries at night, the one who hears him cries with him.

1:4.headline: Those who came for the festivals, or to the Temple?
1:4.body: Rashi reads באי מועד as the pilgrims who came up for the festivals. Ibn Ezra prefers to read מועד as the Temple itself, named so because all Israel met there.

sources.quote: בָּאֵי מוֹעֵד. עוֹלֵי רְגָלִים
sources.says: Rashi says these are the pilgrims.

sources.quote: והטוב בעיני שהוא המקדש, ונקרא מועד בעבור היות כל ישראל נועדים שם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra prefers that it is the Temple, called מועד because all Israel gathered there.

1:6.headline: A 'full' spelling for a full chase
1:6.body: Rashi says the word for 'pursuer' is always written without the ו in Scripture, but here it is spelled in full. They were chased with a complete chase. A poet built on this: 'full is my pursuit, and lacking is my year of redemption'.

sources.quote: כָּל "רֹדֵף" שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא חָסֵר, וְזֶה מָלֵא, שֶׁנִּרְדְּפוּ רְדִיפָה שְׁלֵמָה
sources.says: Rashi says every רדף in Scripture is spelled short, but this one is full, because they were chased with a full chase.

sources.quote: עַל כֵּן יָסַד הַפַּיָּט, "מָלֵא רֻדַּפְתִּי וְחָסְרָה שְׁנַת גְּאוּלַי
sources.says: Rashi says a liturgical poet therefore wrote 'full is my pursuit, and lacking is my year of redemption'.

1:8.headline: Sent wandering, or made a thing to shake heads at?
1:8.body: Rashi reads לנידה as exile, from 'a wanderer' (נע ונד). Ibn Ezra reads it as mockery, from shaking the head (מנוד ראש), which he ties to the same root.

sources.quote: לְנִידָה. לְגוֹלָה, לְשׁוֹן "נָע וָנָד
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'to exile', as in 'a wanderer'.

sources.quote: לנידה – ללעג, כמו "מנוד ראש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'to mockery', as in shaking the head.

1:8.headline: Shamed her, brought her down, or made her tears flow
1:8.body: Ibn Ezra gives three readings of הזילוה. They cheapened her, the opposite of honor. Or they brought her down. Or they made her tears flow (תזל).

sources.quote: הזילוה – הפך הכבוד, כמו: "להוציא יקר מזולל", רק הוא משורש אחר. או טעמו: הורידוה, או עשו שתזל דמעתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the opposite of honor, or it means they brought her down, or they made her tears flow.

1:10.headline: Her 'precious things' are Torah scrolls
1:10.body: Rashi says the precious things here are Torah scrolls, which are 'more precious than gold'. While others ran for silver and gold, Ammon and Moab went for the scrolls to burn them, because the Torah bars them from the community.

sources.quote: סִפְרֵי תוֹרוֹת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהֶם "הַנֶּחֱמָדִים מִזָּהָב". הַכֹּל נִפְנוּ לָבוֹז כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב, וְהֵם נִפְנִים עַל סִפְרֵי תוֹרוֹת כְּדֵי לְשָׂרְפָם, לְפִי שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּהֶם "לֹא יָבֹא עַמּוֹנִי
sources.says: Rashi says these are Torah scrolls; everyone went for silver and gold, but Ammon and Moab went to burn the scrolls, because they say 'no Ammonite shall enter'.

1:13.headline: Fire that broke the bones, or scraped them hollow?
1:13.body: Rashi reads וירדנה from רדה, 'subdue': the fire broke each bone. His second reading compares Samson scraping honey into his hands: the fire scooped out the marrow. Ibn Ezra says the word points back to the fire.

sources.quote: וַיִּרֶד אוֹתָהּ, וַיְשַׁבֵּר אוֹתָהּ עַל יְדֵי רִדּוּי וְיִסּוּרִין
sources.says: Rashi says it means He subdued it and broke it through suffering.

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר: "וַיִּרְדֶּנָּה" כְּמוֹ "וַיִּרְדֵּהוּ אֶל כַּפָּיו". הֵרִיק אֶת הַמּוֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi gives another reading, like 'he scraped it into his hands': He emptied out the marrow.

sources.quote: וירדנה – שב אל האש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word refers back to the fire.

1:14.headline: Sins braided like rope, or twined like vines
1:14.body: Rashi says the sins were woven into braids that rose onto my neck, like the Mishnah's word for lacing a bed. Ibn Ezra ties it to שריגים, the tendrils of a vine.

sources.quote: נַעֲשׂוּ קְלִיעוֹת קְלִיעוֹת וְעָלוּ עַל צַוָּארִי, לְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה, אֵין מְסָרְגִין אֶת הַמִּטּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they became braids on my neck, from the Mishnah's word for lacing beds.

sources.quote: ישתרגו – מבנין התפעל, ממשפחת השריגים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word belongs to the family of שריגים, vine tendrils.

1:15.headline: A gathering of troops, or the night set for weeping?
1:15.body: Rashi reads מועד as a set meeting: God summoned armies against me. He also brings the sages' reading. The spies returned on the night of the ninth of Av, and the people's weeping that night was fixed for all generations.

sources.quote: קָרָא עָלַי מוֹעֵד. יְעִידַת גְיָסוֹת לָבֹא עָלָי
sources.says: Rashi says it means an appointed gathering of troops to come against me.

sources.quote: לְכַךְ, אֵירַע חֲזָרָתָן שֶׁל מְרַגְּלִים לֵיל תִּשְׁעָה בְאָב, שֶׁעָלֶיהָ הֻקְבְּעָה בְכִיָּתָן לְדוֹרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi brings the sages: the spies returned on the night of the ninth of Av, and their weeping was fixed for generations.

1:19.headline: Not true friends, only people acting like friends
1:19.body: Ibn Ezra says מאהבים are not the same as אוהבים, friends. Rashi says they only showed themselves as friends. He tells of Ishmaelites who fed the exiles salty food, then gave them skins full of air instead of wine.

sources.quote: למאהבי – איננו כמו: "אוהבי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מאהבי is not like אוהבי, 'my friends'.

sources.quote: לְאוֹתָם שֶׁמַּרְאִים עַצְמָם כְּאוֹהֲבִים
sources.says: Rashi says these are people who show themselves as friends.

sources.quote: וְהָיוּ מוֹצִיאִים לָהֶם מִינֵי מְלוּחִים וְנוֹדוֹת נְפוּחִים כִּסְבוּרִים שֶׁהוּא יַיִן
sources.says: Rashi says they brought out salty foods and inflated skins, which the exiles thought held wine.

1:20.headline: My insides shriveled, or turned murky like mud?
1:20.body: Rashi reads חמרמרו as shriveling, as the Mishnah says of an animal that fell into a fire. Ibn Ezra reads it as turning murky, from חומר, clay, with the last letters doubled.

sources.quote: חֳמַרְמְרוּ. כֻּוְּצוּ, וְיֵשׁ כָּזֶה בִלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה: נָפְלָה לְאוּר, וְנֶחְמְרוּ בְנֵי מֵעֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means shriveled, as in the Mishnah's 'it fell into the fire and its innards shriveled'.

sources.quote: וטעמו כמו: "עכורים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means murky.

sources.quote: והוא מגזרת "חומר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from חומר, clay.

2:1.headline: Zion darkened by a cloud, or lifted up to the clouds?
2:1.body: Rashi reads יעיב as 'darkened', from עב, a cloud. Ibn Ezra says it means God first raised Zion as high as the clouds, and then threw her down.

sources.quote: יַאֲפִיל, כְּמָה דְאַתְּ אָמַר
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'darkened', the way clouds darken the sky.

sources.quote: יש אומרים יעיב מ"עב" כמו יחשיך, והנכון יגביה עד עב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes that some read it as 'darken', but says the better reading is 'raise up to the cloud'.

2:4.headline: Why a bow is 'trodden' rather than drawn
2:4.body: The verse says God 'trod' (דרך) his bow. Rashi explains that a strong bow was bent by stepping on it, so the word for treading fits.

sources.quote: לָשׂוּם רַגְלוֹ עֲלֵיהֶם כְּשֶׁהוּא כוֹפְפָם
sources.says: Rashi says archers put a foot on a strong bow to bend it, so the text uses the word for treading.

2:6.headline: Here חמס means cut down, not violence
2:6.body: The word usually means violence or robbery. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it here as cutting or stripping bare, the way a garden is cut back.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן כְּרִיתָה, וְכֵן: "יַחְמֹס כַּגֶּפֶן"
sources.says: Rashi says it means cutting, and compares 'יחמס כגפן', said of a vine.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ שֶׁגּוֹזְזִין יַרְקוֹת הַגִּנָּה
sources.says: Rashi says 'like a garden' means the way garden greens are cut.

sources.quote: ויחמוס – חשף, נחמסו עקביך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means stripped bare, and cites נחמסו עקביך, 'your heels are bared', from Jeremiah.

2:6.headline: His booth, or his anger calmed? One spelling, two readings
2:6.body: Read with a sin, שכו means God's booth, His dwelling. Rashi notes the spelling also reads 'he calmed': by destroying His house, God calmed His anger against His children.

sources.quote: כְּתִיב, שֶׁשִׁכֵּךְ חֲמָתוֹ עַל בָּנָיו בְּחֻרְבַּן בֵּיתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the word means His dwelling, but its spelling hints that He calmed His anger against His children by destroying His house, as the midrash on Lamentations teaches.

sources.quote: סֻכּוֹ וסֻכָּתוֹ כמו חֻקּוֹ וחֻקָּתוֹ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says סכו is the same as סכתו, 'his booth'.

2:11.headline: Insides that shrivel like guts thrown on a fire
2:11.body: חמרמרו is an unusual doubled word for inner turmoil. Rashi gives an Old French word for it and says it is how innards curl up when thrown into a fire.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁמַּשְׁלִיכָם אָדָם לָאוּר, הֵם כּוֹוְצִים וּמִתְחֲמַרְמְרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it describes intestines that shrink and churn when a person throws them into a fire.

2:14.headline: False prophecy called tasteless, like food without salt
2:14.body: תפל is bland food with no flavor. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say the false prophets' words were like that: they had no טעם, no taste and no sense.

sources.quote: דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם טַעַם
sources.says: Rashi says these are words with no taste, that is, no sense.

sources.quote: וכן היאכל תפל (איוב ו ו) שאין לו טעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares 'can bland food be eaten' in Job, food that has no taste.

2:14.headline: Restore your fortunes, or turn you back from straying?
2:14.body: להשיב שבות is often read as 'bring back the captives'. Rashi reads שבותך here from שובב, 'wayward': the prophets should have set right the people's straying.

sources.quote: לְיַשֵׁר מְשׁוּבוֹתַיִךְ, לְשׁוֹן "שׁוֹבְבָה", "שׁוֹבָבִים"
sources.says: Rashi says it means to straighten your backslidings, from the word for wayward.

2:20.headline: Babies 'of handbreadths': patted infants, or a child measured by hand
2:20.body: Rashi says טפחים are tender babies still raised with their mothers' patting. He adds a teaching of the sages about a mother who measured her son by handbreadths each day.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיְתָה אִמּוֹ מוֹדַדְתּוֹ בִטְפָחִים בְּכָל יוֹם וָיוֹם
sources.says: Rashi explains them as soft children raised by their mothers' patting, and cites the sages on Doeg ben Yosef, whose mother measured him by handbreadths every day.

sources.quote: מגזרת טפח, כמנהג הנשים עם ילדיהם הקטנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from טפח, the way women pat their small children to sleep.

2:22.headline: My terrors, or my neighbors?
2:22.body: Rashi reads מגורי as 'my neighbors', from גור, to live near: bad neighbors who gathered to destroy. Ibn Ezra reads it from fear, as in 'be afraid of the sword'.

sources.quote: שְׁכֻנַי הָרָעִים לְהֵאָסֵף עָלַי
sources.says: Rashi says they are my evil neighbors, who gathered against me to destroy.

sources.quote: מגזרת גורו לכם מפני חרב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra derives it from 'be afraid of the sword' in Job, and notes that some read it as 'the people who live with me'.

3:1.headline: Who is "the man who has seen affliction"?
3:1.body: Rashi says it is Jeremiah: other prophets foretold the Temple's fall, but it fell in his own days. Ibn Ezra allows that any person of Israel may be speaking.

sources.quote: אשר ראה עני מכל הנביאים שנתנבאו על חרבן הבית, שבימיהם לא נחרב הבית, כי אם בימי
sources.says: Rashi says Jeremiah saw more suffering than all the prophets who foretold the Temple's fall, since it fell only in his days.

sources.quote: אם כן יהיה הוא האומר אני הגבר, או יאמר כל אחד מישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that if Jeremiah wrote the book he is the speaker, or else any one of Israel may say it.

3:5.headline: A bitter plant, or the head of Babylon?
3:5.body: ראש can mean a bitter, poisonous plant, as in "ראש and wormwood". A midrash in Rashi reads it as "head": Nebuchadnezzar, with תלאה, weariness, standing for Nebuzaradan, who finished the blow.

sources.quote: כמו "ראש ולענה"
sources.says: Rashi says ראש here is the bitter plant named together with wormwood.

sources.quote: ומדרש אגדה: ראש זה נבוכדנצר בגלות יהויכין. ותלאה, נבוזראדן שגמר המכה
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash that ראש is Nebuchadnezzar in Jehoiachin's exile, and תלאה is Nebuzaradan, who finished the blow in Zedekiah's time.

3:11.headline: Thorns on my road, or a road turned aside?
3:11.body: Rashi reads סורר from סירים, thorns: God scattered thorns on my path. Ibn Ezra prefers the root of Hosea's "stubborn cow" that turns aside.

sources.quote: לשון סירים, קוצים. סורר, קווץ אותם, מפזר קוצים בדרכי
sources.says: Rashi says the word comes from thorns: God spread thorns on my roads.

sources.quote: והישר בעיני שהוא פעל עבר מגזרת כפרה סוררה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some link it to thorns, but he thinks it comes from the root of "a stubborn cow".

3:13.headline: Arrows called the "children" of the quiver
3:13.body: The verse calls the arrows בני אשפתו, "the sons of his quiver". Ibn Ezra says the quiver is pictured as a pregnant womb holding its children.

sources.quote: אשפתו – דימה האשפה לבטן ההרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the quiver is likened to the belly of a pregnant woman.

sources.quote: חצים שנותנין בתוך אשפה
sources.says: Rashi says these are arrows that are put inside a quiver.

3:16.headline: A word found only here: soiled, or turned over in ash?
3:16.body: Ibn Ezra says הכפישני has no twin in Scripture and means "soiled me". Rashi reads it as "turned me over in ashes", like a vessel set upside down.

sources.quote: הכפישני – אין לו אח, והטעם גאלני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no other example and means "he defiled me".

sources.quote: כפה אותי באפר ככלי הכפוי על פיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means he turned me over in ashes like a vessel turned upside down.

3:18.headline: My lasting hope, or my lifeblood?
3:18.body: Rashi reads נצחי as "my world and my hope". Ibn Ezra links it to נצחם in Isaiah, which means blood: the blood that keeps a living being alive.

sources.quote: אבד עולמי וסברי
sources.says: Rashi says it means: my world and my hope are lost.

sources.quote: על הדם שבו יעמד החי נצחו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נצח is used for blood, by which a living being lasts, as in Isaiah 63:3.

3:22.headline: God's kindness has not ended, or we have not ended?
3:22.body: Rashi first reads תמנו as תמו: God's kindnesses never run out. Others read it as "we": because of God's kindness, we were not wiped out for our sins.

sources.quote: כי לא תמנו. כמו כי לא תמו
sources.says: Rashi says תמנו is like תמו, "have not ended".

sources.quote: חסדי ה' הם אשר לא תמנו ולא כלינו בעונינו
sources.says: Rashi brings others who read it as: it is God's kindness that we were not finished off for our sins.

3:65.headline: A shield over the heart, not grief
3:65.body: Rashi reads מגנת לב as a covering over the heart, like a shield, that shuts it in pain. He says those who read it as יגון, grief, are wrong, because the nun is not part of that root.

sources.quote: אוטם הלב, צרה ואנחה, אשר היא כמגן כנגד לבם
sources.says: Rashi says it means a blocking of the heart, trouble and sighing that lie like a shield against their heart.

sources.quote: והמפרשו בלשון תוגה ויגון טועה, שאין נו"ן נופלת בו
sources.says: Rashi says whoever explains it as grief is mistaken, because the nun is not a root letter.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שהוא מן גנון והציל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he thinks it comes from the word for shielding in Isaiah 31:5.

3:65.headline: Your curse on them, or folly on them?
3:65.body: Ibn Ezra reads תאלתך from אלה, a curse: let Your curse be on them. Rashi links it to נואלו, "became fools", as in Isaiah's foolish princes of Zoan.

sources.quote: תאלתך – מגזרת אלה והתי"ו נוסף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from אלה, a curse, with an added tav.

sources.quote: תאלתך. לשון "נואלו שרי צען"
sources.says: Rashi says it is from the same root as "the princes of Zoan have become fools".

4:1.headline: How the gold has dimmed: a rare verb read through Aramaic
4:1.body: יועם is a rare verb. Rashi says it means 'grows dim', using the Aramaic word for a faded color. Ibn Ezra prefers to link it to a verse in Ezekiel about trees that could not outshine a cedar.

sources.quote: יִכְהֶה, כְּמוֹ דְאַתְּ מְתַּרְגֵּם כֵּהָה עַמְיָא
sources.says: Rashi says the word means 'grows dim', as the Aramaic translation renders 'faded' with this word.

sources.quote: והישר בעיני כמו לא עממוהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes some read it as 'darkened' from the Aramaic, but he thinks it is better tied to 'they could not dim him' in Ezekiel 31:8.

4:1.headline: The holy stones spilled in the streets are people
4:1.body: On its face the verse speaks of sacred stones scattered in the streets. Rashi reads them as Zion's children, who shone like gems, and adds a midrash about the blood of King Josiah.

sources.quote: בָּנִים הַמְאִירִים כַּאֲבָנִים טוֹבוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the holy stones are children who shone like precious stones.

sources.quote: כָּל רְבִיעִית דָּם שֶׁיָּצָא מִיֹּאשִׁיָּהוּ
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash that Jeremiah buried each measure of blood that flowed from Josiah's arrow wounds, and read this verse over it.

4:3.headline: Even a fierce beast bares its breast for its young
4:3.body: The word is written תנין, a fierce creature. Rashi says that though it is cruel, it uncovers its breast to feed its hungry young. In the famine, Jerusalem's people put their own lives before their children's.

sources.quote: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאַכְזָרִי הוּא, חָלְצוּ שַׁד
sources.says: Rashi says that though this creature is cruel, it draws out its breast from a covering so its young will not turn away.

sources.quote: שֶׁחַיֵּיהֶם קוֹדְמִים לָהֶם לְחַיֵּי בְנֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the people saw their children crying for bread and gave them none, because their own lives came first.

4:7.headline: Her princes, or her nazirites? Rashi weighs both
4:7.body: נזיריה can come from נזר, a crown, and mean her nobles. Rashi's own view is that it means real nazirites, who let their hair grow long and were especially fair.

sources.quote: שָׂרֶיהָ, כְּמוֹ נֵזֶר וְכֶתֶר
sources.says: Rashi first gives the reading 'her princes', from the word for crown.

sources.quote: וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר, נְזִירֶיהָ מַמָּשׁ, שֶׁהָיוּ מְגֻדְּלֵי שֵׂעָר
sources.says: Rashi says he himself reads it as actual nazirites, who grew their hair long and were very handsome.

4:7.headline: 'Bone' here means their look, their glow
4:7.body: עצם usually means bone or body. Rashi says here it means appearance, as in Exodus 'like the very sky for clearness'. So the line praises how ruddy they looked.

sources.quote: עֶצֶם. לְשׁוֹן מַרְאֶה, כְּמוֹ וּכְעֶצֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם לָטֹהַר
sources.says: Rashi says עצם means appearance, as in 'like the very sky for clearness'.

4:8.headline: A word found nowhere else: skin shriveled onto bone
4:8.body: צפד appears only here in the Bible. Rashi says it means shriveled and stuck together, and that it has no parallel. Ibn Ezra compares it to דבק, 'clung'.

sources.quote: נִקְמַט וְנִתְחַבֵּר, וְאֵין לוֹ דִמְיוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means wrinkled and joined together, and that the word has no parallel.

sources.quote: צפד – כמו דבק, והוא שם לבדו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'clung' and that the word stands alone.

4:9.headline: 'Pierced' covers both the sword and the bloated starving
4:9.body: מדקרים usually means stabbed. Rashi says the word covers both the sword's wound and the bursting belly of someone swollen by hunger.

sources.quote: בֵּין נְפִיחַת רָעָב בֵּין בִּקּוּעַ חֶרֶב קָרוּי דְּקִירָה
sources.says: Rashi says both the swelling of hunger and the splitting of a sword are called piercing.

4:14.headline: Real blind men, or people wandering like the blind?
4:14.body: Rashi takes the word literally: blind people slipped in the blood in the streets. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'like blind men', the way 'a consuming fire' means 'like a fire'.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהָיוּ הָעִוְרִים הוֹלְכִים בַּשּׁוּק
sources.says: Rashi says that when the blind walked through the market their feet slipped in the blood of the slain.

sources.quote: עורים – כעורים, וכן אש אוכלה הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'like blind men', as in 'a consuming fire'.

4:15.headline: Filthy, or taking wing? Two readings of a one-time word
4:15.body: נצו appears only here. Rashi, following Menachem, says it means filth. Ibn Ezra links it to נוצה, a feather: they took wing and fled like birds.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן סִרְחוֹן וְלִכְלוּךְ
sources.says: Rashi says the word means stench and filth, as Menachem explained it.

sources.quote: נצו – יש להם נוצה כעוף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they have feathers like a bird.

4:16.headline: God's 'face' here means His anger
4:16.body: פנים usually means face. Maimonides lists this verse as one where it means anger. Ibn Ezra explains why: anger shows in the face.

sources.quote: במשמעות הזו משתמשים בו רבות במובן של כעס ה' ורוגזו
sources.says: Maimonides says פנים can mean anger, and lists this verse among those where it means God's anger.

sources.quote: פני ה' – זעף, כי בפנים יראה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the face of God here means fury, because fury shows in the face.

sources.quote: פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם
sources.says: Rashi says it means a face of wrath.

4:20.headline: 'The Lord's anointed' here is King Josiah
4:20.body: משיח means anointed, a title for a king. Rashi and the Targum say the anointed one caught in the enemy's pits is King Josiah, whom Jeremiah mourned.

sources.quote: הוּא יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּדִבְרֵי הַיָּמִים
sources.says: Rashi says the anointed one is Josiah, as Chronicles says Jeremiah lamented for him.

sources.quote: מַלְכָּא יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ דַהֲוָה חָבִיב לָנָא
sources.says: The Targum names him as King Josiah, who was dear to the people.

4:21.headline: Edom here stands for Rome
4:21.body: Rashi reads Edom as Rome. He says Jeremiah was foretelling the fall of the Second Temple, which the Romans would destroy.

sources.quote: נִתְנַבֵּא יִרְמְיָהוּ עַל חֻרְבַּן בַּיִת שֵׁנִי, שֶׁיַּחֲרִיבוּהוּ רוֹמִיִּים
sources.says: Rashi says Jeremiah prophesied about the destruction of the Second Temple, which the Romans would destroy.

4:21.headline: 'Laid bare' here means emptied out: Edom will vomit
4:21.body: The root ערה often means to strip bare. Rashi reads it as 'you will vomit', from Rebecca who 'emptied her jar' at the well. Drunk on the cup of punishment, Edom will spill it all out.

sources.quote: וְתָקִיאִי, כְּמוֹ וַתְּעַר כַּדָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'and you will vomit', as in 'she emptied her jar'.

sources.quote: תִּרְוִי וְתִתְרוֹקְנִי
sources.says: The Targum translates 'you will be drunk and be emptied out'.

5:2.headline: Strangers and foreigners are not the same thing
5:2.body: The verse pairs זרים and נכרים. Malbim says a זר is an outsider to some special thing, like a non-priest near holy food. A נכרי is someone from another land.

sources.quote: הזר הוא המוזר והמופרש מאיזה ענין מיוחד
sources.says: Malbim says a זר is someone set apart from a particular matter.

sources.quote: והנכרי הוא מארץ אחרת
sources.says: Malbim says a נכרי is someone from another land, and lists this verse among his examples.

5:6.headline: "We gave a hand" to Egypt: a plea, an oath, or surrender?
5:6.body: Rashi pictures a man falling who reaches out his hand for help. Ibn Ezra says giving a hand is a pledge, like a handshake. Malbim reads it as submitting to a stronger power.

sources.quote: דֶּרֶךְ אָדָם הַנּוֹפֵל וְרוֹצֶה לַעֲמוֹד, מוֹשִׁיט יָד לְמִי שֶׁאֶצְלוֹ לַעֲזוֹר לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a falling man who reaches out to whoever is near to help him up.

sources.quote: ונתינת היד שבועה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says giving the hand means an oath, like striking hands.

sources.quote: נתנו יד. להכנע תחתיו
sources.says: Malbim, citing this verse, says giving a hand means submitting to someone.

5:7.headline: We carry their sins, or their punishment?
5:7.body: עון usually means sin. Metzudat Zion says here it means punishment: the children bear what their fathers earned. Ibn Ezra says the trouble came because the children's sins joined their fathers' sins.

sources.quote: עון. ענין עונש, וכן (איכה ה ז): ואנחנו עונותיהם סבלנו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עון can mean punishment, and gives this verse as an example.

sources.quote: זאת הרעה הבאה עלינו בעבור עונותינו שהתחברו עם עונות אבותינו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the evil came because our sins were joined to our fathers' sins.

5:9.headline: "With our souls": by ourselves, or at the risk of our lives?
5:9.body: Ibn Ezra first reads it as "we ourselves": once our servants brought our bread, now we must. He prefers a second reading, shared by Rashi: we fetch bread at the risk of our lives.

sources.quote: בתחלה היו עבדינו מביאים לחמנו ועתה אנחנו בעצמנו. והישר בעיני שטעמו בסכנת נפשנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives both readings and says the right one is 'at the risk of our lives'.

sources.quote: בְּסַכָּנַת נַפְשֵׁנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means at the risk of our lives.

5:10.headline: The word for burning skin is also the word for pity
5:10.body: נכמרו means heated. Rashi says hungry skin heats up and shrivels, like any hide that is heated. The same verb describes Joseph's pity welling up, and Metzudat Zion says it is used for compassion.

sources.quote: נִתְחַמְּמוּ וְנִקְמְטוּ קְמָטִים קְמָטִים מִפְּנֵי זַלְעֲפוֹת רָעָב
sources.says: Rashi says the skin grew hot and wrinkled from the burning hunger.

sources.quote: נִתְחַמְּמוּ, לְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי
sources.says: Rashi says the word means grew hot, and is Aramaic.

sources.quote: נכמרו. נתחממו, כמו (איכה ה י) עורנו כתנור נכמרו, והוא ענין חמלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means grew hot, as in this verse, and is used for compassion.

5:10.headline: The burning of hunger, or its storm?
5:10.body: Rashi says זלעפות is a word for burning, as in Psalms' burning wind. Rashi also reports that Menachem read it as a storm or shudder.

sources.quote: זַלְעֲפוֹת רָעָב. כְּמוֹ "וְרוּחַ זִלְעָפוֹת", לְשׁוֹן שְׂרֵפָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word for burning, as in Psalms 11:6.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פָּתַר אוֹתוֹ לְשׁוֹן ״שַׁעַר קָטֶב״
sources.says: Rashi reports that Menachem explained it as a storm, and lists this verse with it.

5:12.headline: Hanged by their own hands, or by the slaves' hands?
5:12.body: Ibn Ezra reads בידם as the princes hanged by their arms. He reports others who say it means by the hands of the slaves named in verse 8.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים כי בידם שב אל העבדים הנזכרים למעלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that 'by their hand' refers back to the slaves mentioned above.

5:13.headline: Young men made to carry millstones, or to grind?
5:13.body: Rashi says the enemy loaded millstones on the captives' shoulders to wear them out. Ibn Ezra reads טחון as the act of grinding: the young men were taken to grind grain.

sources.quote: הָיוּ נוֹתְנִים עַל כְּתֵפֵיהֶם רֵחַיִם וּמַשָׂאוֹת כְּדֵי לְיַגְּעָם
sources.says: Rashi says the enemies put millstones and loads on their shoulders to exhaust them.

sources.quote: בחורים לטחון, ויהיה טחון שם הפועל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the young men were taken to grind, with טחון as the act of grinding.

5:14.headline: The city gate was the elders' court
5:14.body: Elders leaving the gate means more than an empty square. Malbim says the gate was where judges sat, and cites this verse. Ibn Ezra says the elders used to sit in Jerusalem's gates.

sources.quote: והשער היה מקום מושב השופטים
sources.says: Malbim says the gate was the place where the judges sat, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: מנהגם היה לשבת בשערי ירושלים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the elders' custom was to sit in the gates of Jerusalem.

5:16.headline: נא here means "now", not "please"
5:16.body: נא is often read as please. Ibn Ezra says that everywhere in the Bible it means now, and uses "woe to us now" from this verse as an example.

sources.quote: כבר פירשתי כי כל נא במקרא כמו עתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says every נא in the Bible means 'now', and lists this verse.

sources.quote: ומלת נא כמו עתה וכן "הנה נא זקנתי" (בראשית כז ב) "אוי נא לנו"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra again says נא means now, citing this verse.

5:19.headline: God "sits" means God lasts and does not change
5:19.body: ישב usually means sit. Maimonides says that said of God it means lasting forever without any change, and gives this verse. Radak reads it the same way: you endure forever.

sources.quote: הקיים לעד והיציב שאינו משתנה באף אופן מאופני השינוי
sources.says: Maimonides says that when sitting is said of God, as in this verse, it means He endures forever and does not change in any way.

sources.quote: יושב: קים נצח, וכן אתה יי' לעולם תשב
sources.says: Radak says יושב means existing forever, as in this verse.

5:19.headline: God's throne is His greatness, not a seat
5:19.body: Maimonides says a throne for God cannot be a thing outside Him. He uses this verse, where the throne lasts as long as God does, to show that the throne means His glory and greatness.

sources.quote: מה שמורה שהוא דבר שאינו נבדל ממנו
sources.says: Maimonides says this verse shows the throne is not separate from God.

sources.quote: לפיכך הכוונה ב"כסא" כאן ובכל מקום דומה לו – תפארתו וגדולתו
sources.says: Maimonides says that 'throne' here and in similar places means God's glory and greatness.

5:22.headline: Does the book end in despair, or in protest?
5:22.body: Ibn Ezra first reads it as: bring us back quickly, unless you have rejected us. He prefers: even if you rejected us for our sins, your anger has already gone too far. Rashi reads a protest: our sin did not call for so much anger.

sources.quote: והישר בעיני להיותו כי אם מאוס מאסתנו בעונינו כבר קצפת עלינו יותר מדאי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the best reading is: if you rejected us for our sins, you have already been angry with us too much.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁחָטָאנוּ לֹא הָיָה לְךָ לְהַרְבּוֹת קֶצֶף עַד מְאֹד
sources.says: Rashi says that because we sinned you should not have raged so greatly.
